1F (Number Theory)

Words: 79 Articles: 1
Paper 3 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 79
1F OurBigBook.com
Apply the reciprocal-and-integer-part algorithm for the continued fraction. The successive complete quotients after the integer part two are (7​+2)/3, (7​+1)/2, (7​+1)/3, and 7​+2. Their integer parts are 1,1,1,4, and taking the next reciprocal repeats the first complete quotient. Therefore
7​=[2;1,1,1,4​].​
(1)
The first four continued fraction convergents are 2,3,5/2,8/3. The last gives 82−7⋅32=1. Squaring its unit 8+37​ gives 127+487​, whose norm is again one. Thus two positive solutions of the Pell equation are
(x,y)=(8,3),(127,48).​
(2)
Direct verification gives 1272−7⋅482=16129−16128=1.

2F (Topics in Analysis)

Words: 205 Articles: 1
Paper 3 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 205
2F OurBigBook.com
The polynomial form of Runge theorem says that a function holomorphic on a neighbourhood of a compact set K⊂C with connected complement can be approximated uniformly on K by polynomials.
For n≥3, take
Kn​={0}∪{z:1/n≤∣z∣≤1−1/n, 0≤argz≤2π−1/n}.
(3)
The complement is connected: the missing angular sector connects the inner disk to the exterior, and removing the single point zero from the inner disk does not disconnect it. On a neighbourhood of the annular sector choose an analytic logarithm with arguments between −1/(2n) and 2π−1/(2n). Its exponential exp(3logz/2) agrees with the prescribed function on the sector. On a disjoint small neighbourhood of zero prescribe the analytic function zero. These two neighbourhoods define a holomorphic function gn​ near Kn​ with gn​=f on Kn​.
By Runge theorem, choose a polynomial pn​ with supKn​​∣pn​−gn​∣<1/n. Every fixed nonzero point of the disk eventually belongs to all Kn​, including points on the positive real axis; zero belongs to every Kn​. Consequently
pn​(z)⟶f(z)for every z∈D.​
(4)
Each polynomial restricts to an analytic function on D. The excluded sector lies immediately below the positive axis and shrinks with n, so the construction correctly preserves the chosen value on the branch cut. It gives pointwise convergence, not local uniform convergence across that cut. This is pointwise approximation by a Runge exhaustion.

3G (Geometry of Group Actions)

Words: 149 Articles: 1
Paper 3 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 149
3G OurBigBook.com
For a plane crystallographic group, the translation subgroup consists of translations by vectors in a rank-two lattice Λ; the lattice is this additive group of translation vectors. The point group is the image under the linear-part homomorphism G→O(2), equivalently G/Λ. Conjugating a translation by an isometry with linear part A gives translation by Av, so every point-group element preserves Λ.
Choose a lattice basis. A point-group rotation is represented in that basis by an integral matrix, because it maps lattice vectors to lattice vectors, and its inverse does likewise. The trace is therefore an integer. In an orthonormal basis the same rotation has trace 2cosθ, which lies between minus two and two. Hence 2cosθ∈{−2,−1,0,1,2}. The value two gives the identity, while the other values give angles π, ±2π/3, ±π/2, or ±π/3. Thus every nonidentity rotation has order
2,3,4, or 6.​
(5)
This proves the crystallographic restriction theorem from the lattice action rather than assuming the classification of wallpaper groups.

4G (Coding and Cryptography)

Words: 170 Articles: 1
Paper 3 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 170
4G OurBigBook.com
The polynomials are over F2​, and multiplication gives gh=X7+1=X7−1. A cyclic code of length seven generated by a degree-three polynomial has dimension 7−3=4: the multiples ag with dega<4 are distinct representatives, so its rank is four.
The root α has order seven in F8×​: it is neither zero nor one, and the multiplicative group has prime order seven. A weight-one word cannot vanish at α. A weight-two word Xi+Xj, with distinct indices between zero and six, cannot vanish either, because that would give αi−j=1. Every codeword vanishes at α, so its nonzero weight is at least three. Since g itself has weight three,
dmin​=3.​
(6)
From α3=α+1 obtain α4=α2+α and α5=α2+α+1. Therefore r(α)=α5+α3+α=α2+α=α4. The one-bit error X4 has precisely this syndrome, so correcting it gives
c(X)=X5+X4+X3+X=g(X)(X2+X).​
(7)
Its distance from the received word is one. The minimum distance three makes this nearest codeword unique: two codewords each at distance one from the received word would be at distance at most two from each other.

5I (Statistical Modelling)

Words: 189 Articles: 1
Paper 3 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 189
5I OurBigBook.com
Write S(β)=∑ij​μij​(β). Ignoring only terms independent of β, the Poisson log-likelihood is ℓP​=∑yij​logμij​−S(β). The multinomial model is defined on the constraint S(β)=n, since its probabilities must sum to one. On this constraint its full log-likelihood satisfies
ℓM​(β)=ℓP​(β)+n−nlogn+log(n!),
(8)
where both likelihoods include the same −∑log(yij​!) terms. Thus they differ by a constant on the admissible multinomial parameter set.
If the Poisson maximum-likelihood estimator has S(β​)=n, it is feasible for the multinomial problem, and no feasible parameter can have a larger likelihood than it. Consequently it is also a multinomial maximum. With the usual uniqueness and identifiability assumption,
β​=β∗,y​ij​=yij∗​.​
(9)
Without uniqueness, the precise conclusion is that β​ is a multinomial maximizer; arbitrary independently chosen maximizers need not be identical. This qualification is necessary for a general unspecified parametrization.
In a log-linear generalized linear model with an unrestricted intercept, differentiation with respect to that intercept gives ∑(yij​−μ​ij​)=0. Thus the fitted total automatically equals n. One can fit independent Poisson cell counts using the usual GLM machinery and recover the multinomial fitted probabilities as μ​ij​/n. The result is constrained Poisson and multinomial likelihood equivalence, not an assertion that the sampling experiments themselves are identical.

6B (Mathematical Biology)

Words: 126 Articles: 1
Paper 3 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 126
6B OurBigBook.com
The pair-birth rate here is the constant immigration rate λ, while deaths occur at total rate βn. This interpretation is fixed by the requested mean formula. With Pn​(t)=Pr(Nt​=n) and Pj​=0 for j<0, the master equation is
Pn′​=λPn−2​+β(n+1)Pn+1​−(λ+βn)Pn​.​
(10)
The Markov jump-process generator acts as Lf(n)=λ[f(n+2)−f(n)]+βn[f(n−1)−f(n)]. Taking f(n)=n gives m′=2λ−βm, hence
m(t)=β2λ​(1−e−βt)+n0​e−βt.​
(11)
For the second moment s=ENt2​, the two jumps give s′=4λm+4λ−2βs+βm. Differentiating V=s−m2 therefore yields V′=4λ+βm−2βV. Substitution of the mean and solution of this scalar linear equation give
V(t)=β3λ​+(V(0)−3λ/β)e−2βt+(n0​−2λ/β)(e−βt−e−2βt).
(12)
Thus V(t)→3λ/β, assuming β>0 and finite initial second moment. This is pair immigration with linear deaths; births at rate λn would be a different model and would not give the printed mean.

7E (Dynamical Systems)

Words: 132 Articles: 1
Paper 3 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 132
7E OurBigBook.com
A form of the Poincaré-Bendixson theorem states that a nonempty omega-limit set of a forward orbit of a C1 planar autonomous vector field, contained in a compact region and containing no equilibrium, is a periodic orbit.
Set ρ=x2+y2. Direct calculation gives
ρ˙​=2ρ(1−ρ)−4k2x2y2,2ρ−(2+k2)ρ2≤ρ˙​≤2ρ(1−ρ),
(13)
because 0≤x2y2≤ρ2/4. At the inner boundary ρ=2/(2+k2) the flow points into or along the annulus, and at the outer boundary ρ=1 it does likewise. Smoothness and these inequalities make the compact annulus forward invariant.
For nonzero (x,y), write x=ρ​cosθ, y=ρ​sinθ. Then
θ˙=ρxy˙​−yx˙​=1−4k2ρ​sin4θ≥1−4k2​>0
(14)
throughout the annulus. Hence it contains no equilibrium. Any orbit starting there remains compactly trapped, has a nonempty omega-limit set, and the Poincaré-Bendixson theorem supplies the required periodic orbit in the stated annulus. For k=0 the annulus reduces to ρ=1 itself, and there θ˙=1, giving the periodic orbit directly.

i OurBigBook.com
Let u1​,u2​ be a local fundamental pair at zero, including a logarithmic Frobenius solution if the exponents are resonant. Any other independent pair on a common branch domain has w1​=au1​+bu2​ and w2​=cu1​+du2​ with constant coefficients and ad−bc=0. Bilinearity and antisymmetry of the Wronskian give
W(w1​,w2​)=(ad−bc)W(u1​,u2​).​
(15)
Thus changing the independent branches multiplies the principal-pair Wronskian by a nonzero constant, once the branches are continued onto the same domain.

ii

Words: 128 Articles: 1
8B OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 128
ii OurBigBook.com
For the second-order Fuchsian equation represented by the Papperitz symbol, the coefficient of w′ is
p(z)=z1−α−α′​+z−11−γ−γ′​.
(16)
This follows from the sums of local exponents at its two finite regular singular points. Abel's Wronskian identity, obtained by differentiating w1​w2′​−w1′​w2​ and using the differential equation, gives W′=−pW. Thus, on every branch domain avoiding zero and one,
dzd​[z1−α−α′(1−z)1−γ−γ′W(z)]=0.
(17)
The normalized expression is locally constant. Its analytic continuation around either singularity is unchanged: the power factors cancel the determinant of the local monodromy, equivalently the integral of −p around that singularity. It therefore defines a single-valued holomorphic function on the punctured plane, locally constant near both punctures. Those punctures are removable, so the normalized expression extends to an entire function. This argument also covers resonant exponents and avoids assuming two pure power solutions in that case.

iii

Words: 93 Articles: 1
8B OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 93
iii OurBigBook.com
Let H=z1−α−α′(1−z)1−γ−γ′W. The exponent-sum relation gives 2−α−α′−γ−γ′=1+β+β′. Therefore the assumed boundedness of z1+β+β′W at infinity makes H bounded there, up to a fixed nonzero branch factor. By part (ii), H is entire and hence bounded also on compact sets. Liouville theorem makes it a constant A, giving
W(z)=Azα+α′−1(1−z)γ+γ′−1.​
(18)
Independence forces A=0: if the Wronskian vanished, uniqueness for the second-order linear equation at an ordinary point would make the two solutions dependent. In fact the differential identity in part (ii) already proves constancy; the boundedness hypothesis supplies the requested Liouville route as well.

Put Ij​=mj​rj2​ and K=ω2r1​r2​. The Euler-Lagrange equations are I1​ϕ¨​1​=Ksinψ and I2​ϕ¨​2​=−Ksinψ, where ψ=ϕ2​−ϕ1​. Adding shows that I1​ϕ˙​1​+I2​ϕ˙​2​ is conserved. Subtracting gives the equation of a simple pendulum
ψ¨​=−k2sinψ,k2=ω2r1​r2​(m1​r12​1​+m2​r22​1​).​
(19)
The relative equilibria are ψ=0 and ψ=π modulo 2π. The relative energy ψ˙​2/2+k2(1−cosψ) has a strict minimum at zero, proving stability there. Linearization gives η¨​=−k2η near zero and η¨​=k2η near π, so the latter is unstable. The small-oscillation period is 2π/k. These are equilibria of the relative angle; a nonzero conserved total angular momentum permits common rotation of both particles.

10A (Cosmology)

Words: 227 Articles: 1
Paper 3 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 227
10A OurBigBook.com
Chemical equilibrium gives μHe​=2μp​+2μn​, since the photon chemical potential is zero. Set A=(2πmp​kT/h2)3/2. The degeneracies and approximate masses give prefactors 2A,2A,8A for protons, neutrons and helium. Thus
nHe​np2​nn2​​=2A3e−BHe​/kT.​
(20)
Here the binding energy uses 2mp​+2mn​−mHe​; the PDF prints 2nn​ in that mass relation, a dimensional typo.
Baryon conservation gives nB​∝a−3. In adiabatic expansion without photon-producing entropy release, T∝a−1 and nγ​∝T3∝a−3, so η=nB​/nγ​ stays constant. This statement is for that epoch; entropy transfer such as electron-positron annihilation modifies the photon normalization.
Since the density ratio equals nB3​Xp2​Xn2​/XHe​, substitution of the given photon density yields
XHe​Xp2​Xn2​​=32η−3​(2π​)3/2(kTmp​c2​)9/2e−BHe​/kT.​
(21)
At mp​c2≃938 MeV, BHe​=30 MeV and kT=0.3 MeV, the right side is about 1.22×10−29η−3. Unity therefore corresponds to η≃2.3×10−10, illustrating the stated very rough temperature estimate for a cosmological baryon-to-photon ratio of order 10−10 to 10−9. A numerical value of η is necessary; it is not specified in the question. The exponential makes the temperature estimate far less sensitive than the ratio itself to order-one prefactors.
Actual helium synthesis must proceed through light intermediates. The deuterium bottleneck persists because deuterium's much smaller binding energy allows the abundant high-energy photon tail to destroy it. Only at a lower temperature do enough deuterons survive to initiate efficient reactions leading to helium. Direct four-nucleon assembly at the equilibrium temperature is ineffective.

Solution

Words: 287
11F OurBigBook.com
The Chinese remainder theorem says that for pairwise coprime positive moduli mi​, the map Z/(∏mi​)→∏i​Z/mi​ is an isomorphism; in particular prescribed residues have a unique solution modulo the product.
Write n=pem, with e≥2 and (p,m)=1. Choose z≡1+pe−1(modpe) and z≡1(modm). The Chinese remainder theorem supplies z. The binomial theorem gives zp≡1(modpe), since every nonconstant term is divisible by pe; also zp≡1(modm). Thus zp≡1(modn), whereas z≡1(modn). Its multiplicative order is exactly p.
For odd n=∏piei​​ define the Jacobi symbol (a/n)=∏i​(a/pi​)ei​, using the Legendre symbol, with (a/1)=1. It is zero if a shares a prime factor with n. For example (2/9)=(2/3)2=1, but the square residues modulo nine are 0,1,4,7, so two is not a square.
For positive odd coprime u,v, Jacobi reciprocity is
(u/v)=(−1)(u−1)(v−1)/4(v/u).​
(22)
Factor u=∏piai​​ and v=∏qjbj​​ and multiply quadratic reciprocity for each prime pair. Its sign exponent is ∑i,j​ai​bj​(pi​−1)(qj​−1)/4. For odd numbers, (rs−1)/2≡(r−1)/2+(s−1)/2(mod2), so this exponent has the same parity as (u−1)(v−1)/4. Multiplicativity of the Legendre symbol gives the two Jacobi products, proving the formula. If u,v are not coprime, both sides of the displayed reciprocity equality are zero.
For the previously constructed z, every prime divisor of n sees residue one, so (z/n)=1. But p∤(n−1)/2, because p∣n and p is odd. The order-p unit therefore has z(n−1)/2≡1(modn). This supplies a unit failing the proposed test.
Finally the passing units form the kernel of the homomorphism
F:(Z/nZ)×⟶(Z/nZ)×,F(a)=a(n−1)/2(a/n)−1.
(23)
Multiplicativity makes this a homomorphism, and the failing unit shows its kernel is proper. A proper subgroup has index at least two. Hence the test fails on at least half the units modulo n.

Solution

i OurBigBook.com
The Liouville approximation theorem states that if a real irrational algebraic number α has degree d, there is c>0 such that ∣α−p/q∣≥c/qd for every integer p and positive integer q.
Choose its irreducible polynomial F∈Z[X] of degree d. Since α is irrational, F(p/q)=0; after multiplication by qd it is a nonzero integer. Hence ∣F(p/q)∣≥q−d. On [α−1,α+1] the polynomial derivative has a finite bound M>0. For ∣p/q−α∣<1, the mean value theorem gives ∣F(p/q)∣≤M∣p/q−α∣, proving the required bound with c=1/M. For more distant rationals, the bound holds with c≤1. Taking c=min{1,1/M} covers every rational and proves the theorem.

ii OurBigBook.com
Let ξn+1​=an+1​+1/(an+2​+⋯) be the complete quotient. Iterating the fractional-linear formula for a continued fraction gives
x=qn​ξn+1​+qn−1​pn​ξn+1​+pn−1​​.
(24)
The supplied determinant identity and ξn+1​>an+1​ therefore imply
​x−qn​pn​​​=qn​(qn​ξn+1​+qn−1​)1​<qn​qn+1​1​.​
(25)
The positive partial quotients ensure increasing denominators tending to infinity; the same determinant identity makes the even and odd convergents nested, giving their common limit x. The displayed formula follows by passing to the limit in the finite-tail identity.
An explicit choice is an​=10n! for every n≥1. The recurrence gives qn​≤∏j=1n​(aj​+1)≤2n10∑j=1n​j!. For n≥2, ∑j=1n​j!≤2n!, so log10​qn​≤3n!. Consequently an+1​=10(n+1)!≥qn(n+1)/3​ and
0<​x−qn​pn​​​<qn−2−(n+1)/3​.
(26)
First x is irrational: if x=P/Q, the nonzero difference from a convergent is at least 1/(Qqn​), contradicting the error bound once qn+1​>Q. If x were algebraic of any fixed degree d, the last displayed upper bound would eventually be smaller than c/qnd​ for the positive constant in part (i), since qn​→∞. This contradicts the Liouville approximation theorem. Thus this explicit continued fraction is transcendental.

The term γn(n0​−n) is logistic population growth, with carrying density n0​ and low-density growth rate γn0​. The cell flux is −Dn​∇n+χn∇C: its first part is diffusion down the density gradient, and its second is chemotaxis toward higher chemical concentration. Taking minus its divergence gives the two transport terms. Chemical production is proportional to cell density at rate αn, degradation is first order at rate βC, and the chemical diffuses with coefficient Dc​. All the given positive signs correspond to growth, attraction, production, degradation and ordinary diffusion respectively.

The positive homogeneous equilibrium is n=n0​, C=αn0​/β. For spatially constant perturbations u,v, linearization gives u˙=−γn0​u and v˙=αu−βv. The triangular matrix has eigenvalues −γn0​ and −β, both negative, proving asymptotic stability to homogeneous perturbations. The other homogeneous equilibrium, zero population and zero chemical, has positive population eigenvalue γn0​ and is not the desired stable state.

For a Laplacian mode with ∇2=−k2, the linearized chemotaxis system is
dtd​(vu​)=(−γn0​−Dn​k2α​χn0​k2−β−Dc​k2​)(vu​).
(27)
Its trace is negative for all k. Writing s=k2, its determinant is
Dn​Dc​s2+(βDn​+γn0​Dc​−χαn0​)s+βγn0​.
(28)
Instability occurs when this determinant is negative, because then one real eigenvalue is positive. A quadratic with positive leading and constant coefficients is negative for some s>0 precisely when its middle coefficient is negative and its discriminant positive. These conditions combine to
χαn0​>βDn​+γn0​Dc​+2βγn0​Dn​Dc​​.​
(29)
This proves the printed threshold. In a bounded spatial domain, only its permitted Laplacian eigenmodes are available; the continuous-k threshold describes the onset when wavenumbers can vary freely.

kc2​=Dn​Dc​βγn0​​​,kc​=(Dn​Dc​βγn0​​)1/4.​

The mode is neutral exactly at onset and grows when the chemotactic coefficient increases beyond that threshold.

Choose A=B=σ/r in the proposed Lyapunov function. The cubic terms cancel and direct differentiation gives
V˙=−σx2+2σxy−rσ​y2−rσb​z2=−σ(x−y)2−σ(1/r−1)y2−rσb​z2.
(31)
For 0<r<1 this is negative definite, while V is positive definite and radially unbounded. Finite-dimensional equivalence of these positive quadratic forms gives V˙≤−cV for some c>0. Thus V(t)≤V(0)e−ct, every solution remains bounded and exists for all forward times, and every solution tends to zero. Therefore the origin is globally asymptotically stable, indeed exponentially stable.

ii OurBigBook.com
The centre manifold theorem says that near an equilibrium of a sufficiently smooth finite-dimensional vector field, there is a locally invariant centre manifold tangent to the generalized eigenspace of eigenvalues with zero real part. It can be represented as a graph over that space, with graph value and derivative zero at the equilibrium; the dynamics on it determine the local centre-direction behaviour. For parameter-dependent systems the parameters may be adjoined as variables with zero derivative, producing an extended centre manifold.
At r=1, the linearization has the x,y block (−σ1​σ−1​) and the independent eigenvalue −b. Its other eigenvalues are zero and −(σ+1). Hence the equilibrium is nonhyperbolic, the stable subspace has dimension two, and the non-extended centre subspace has dimension one. A centre eigenvector is (1,1,0).

The remaining tail of the ordinal interval has an order type ρ with α=ωα0​a0​+ρ; maximality implies ρ<ωα0​. If ρ>0, repeat the construction on it. The leading exponents strictly decrease, and there is no infinite strictly decreasing sequence of ordinals: its set of values would have a least member followed by a smaller one. α=ωα0​a0​+ωα1​a1​+⋯+ωαn​an​,α0​>⋯>αn​,aj​∈N>0​.​

The first exponent is determined by the preceding band, the first coefficient by maximality, and the tail by the ordinal interval left after that initial segment. Recursion therefore proves uniqueness of every exponent and coefficient. The PDF's second coefficient is printed α1​ rather than a1​; the stated natural-number coefficients and the construction identify the intended expression.
For the final assertion, powers of ω are additively indecomposable: if τ<ωη, then τ+ωη=ωη for η>0. One proves this by induction on η. At a successor, bound τ by a finite multiple of ωη−1 and use the supremum over all such multiples; at a limit, bound τ by a smaller power and use continuity. For η=0 the only possible τ is zero. Thus a smaller leading exponent is absorbed when a larger-leading ordinal is added on its right. If β,γ have unequal leading exponents, either β+γ=γ or γ+β=β. If their leading exponents coincide, the leading coefficient of either sum is the sum of their two positive leading coefficients; it exceeds each coefficient, so neither absorption equality holds. Zero is never commensurable with an ordinal. Consequently commensurability is exactly equality of the leading exponent, equivalently membership of both positive ordinals in one of the stated bands.

Hall marriage theorem says that a bipartite graph with equal finite vertex-class sizes has a perfect matching exactly when ∣Γ(A)∣≥∣A∣ for every A⊆X. Necessity follows because distinct matched partners of vertices of A belong to Γ(A).
For sufficiency, induct on n, the case n=1 being immediate. If a nonempty proper A is tight, ∣Γ(A)∣=∣A∣, the induced graph between A and Γ(A) satisfies Hall's condition and has a matching by induction. The remaining graph also satisfies it: for B⊆X∖A, the condition on A∪B gives ∣Γ(B)∖Γ(A)∣≥∣B∣. Induction gives the second matching, and their union is perfect. Otherwise every nonempty proper subset has strictly more neighbours. Choose an edge xy and remove its ends. Every remaining nonempty subset loses at most one neighbour and originally had at least one spare neighbour, so Hall's condition survives. Induction matches the remaining graph, and restoring xy completes the proof.
The last argument also proves flexibility under the strict condition: it works for every selected edge, so every vertex is flexible. The case n=1 is again immediate.
Now suppose only that a perfect matching exists. Choose a minimal nonempty tight set A⊆X; such a set exists since X is tight. Every nonempty proper subset of A satisfies the strict condition in the induced graph on A,Γ(A). Hence every edge from a vertex of A extends to a matching of that induced graph. There are no edges from A to the complement of Γ(A). Restrict the original perfect matching to the complementary vertex classes and append it to this new induced matching. This makes every vertex of A flexible in the whole graph, proving that at least one flexible vertex exists.
For the requested counterexample, take X={x1​,x2​,x3​,x4​} and Y={y1​,y2​,y3​,y4​}. Join x1​ only to y1​,y2​, and join each of x2​,x3​,x4​ to all of y2​,y3​,y4​. There is a perfect matching using x1​y1​ and a matching of the remaining complete bipartite graph. The unique minimum-degree vertex is x1​, of degree two, but x1​y2​ cannot occur in a perfect matching because y1​ has no other neighbour. Thus no minimum-degree vertex is flexible, while the other three vertices are flexible.

The quotient map p is open because p−1(p(U))=⋃g​gU is open. Each restriction p:gU→p(U) is a continuous open bijection and hence a homeomorphism. With concatenation meaning first the first loop and then the second, the second lift from gx0​ is g times the lift from x0​, so the endpoint is ghx0​. This proves the homomorphism property. The Arzelà-Ascoli theorem for C([0,1]) states that a family has compact closure in the uniform norm exactly when it is uniformly bounded and equicontinuous. To prove sufficiency, choose a countable dense set. From any sequence of functions, successive subsequence extraction at each dense point and a diagonal selection give convergence at all those points. Given ε>0, equicontinuity gives a common δ; cover the interval by finitely many δ-balls centered at dense points. On a sufficiently late tail the functions differ by less than ε/3 at those finitely many centres, and equicontinuity makes each of the other two differences less than ε/3. Thus the selected subsequence is uniformly Cauchy. Completeness of C([0,1]) gives a continuous uniform limit. In a metric space this proves compactness of the closure. Conversely, a compact family has finite uniform ε-nets. The finitely many net functions are bounded and uniformly continuous; approximation by them gives a common bound and equicontinuity for the family. This proves both directions.
For f∈SN​, a positive interior maximum would have f′=0 and f′′≤0, contradicting f′′=f>0. A negative interior minimum likewise contradicts f′′=f<0. The endpoint bounds therefore give ∣f∣≤N everywhere.
Now put w=f′. Differentiating the equation, using the stipulated third derivative, gives w′′=w+2ww′. At an interior extremum of w, w′=0, so w′′=w. The same maximum/minimum argument and the derivative endpoint bounds imply ∣f′∣=∣w∣≤N. Consequently ∣f(x)−f(y)∣≤N∣x−y∣ by the mean value theorem. Thus SN​ is uniformly bounded and equicontinuous, and the theorem makes it relatively compact, hence totally bounded in C([0,1]). Its closure need not be asserted to remain thrice differentiable.

A Markov control chooses its action from the current time and state, a=u(k,x), rather than the full past. It gives transition probabilities Pku​(x,y)=P(y∣k,x,u(k,x)), hence a time-inhomogeneous Markov chain.
For any admissible control, the given inequality and conditional expectation imply
V(k,Xk​)≤c(k,Xk​,Ak​)+E[V(k+1,Xk+1​)∣Fk​].
(63)
Take expectations and sum from zero to n−1. The value terms telescope, and V(n,Xn​)=C(Xn​) gives V(0,x)≤Ex​[∑k<n​c(k,Xk​,Ak​)+C(Xn​)]. For u∗ every inequality is equality, so its cost is exactly V(0,x) and it achieves the lower bound. Thus u∗ is optimal. Boundedness of V and the usual integrability of the costs justify these expectations; the argument even compares it with history-dependent controls.
For the cards, let r,b be the remaining red and black counts, m=r+b≥2. Betting now succeeds with probability q(r,b)=r(r−1)/[m(m−1)]. For m≥3, elementary simplification gives
mr​q(r−1,b)+mb​q(r,b−1)=q(r,b),
(64)
with zero-probability transitions omitted when a colour count vanishes. Thus continuing one reveal has exactly the same conditional winning probability as betting now. The backward value function for maximal success probability is q at m=2, and induction makes it q at every earlier state: the stop and continue values coincide. Equivalently the conditional success probabilities are a bounded martingale, and every permitted stopping time is bounded by the time at which two cards remain.
Therefore any adapted betting rule that makes exactly one bet while at least two cards remain is optimal; there is no strictly advantageous moment. Betting immediately is one simple optimal rule, with winning probability 26⋅25/(52⋅51)=25/102. The stake size only rescales a fixed payoff, and does not alter this comparison. This is unchanging betting probability under sampling without replacement; allowing the player never to bet would be a different problem.

The heat kernel is Ht​(x)=(4πt)−1/2e−x2/(4t), so the homogeneous solution for smooth bounded data is u(t,x)=(Ht​∗g)(x). Differentiating under the integral gives the heat equation, and the approximate-identity property gives the initial value.
For a tempered distribution, its derivative is defined by ⟨T′,ψ⟩=−⟨T,ψ′⟩ for every Schwartz test function. A fundamental solution of a constant-coefficient operator P is a distribution E satisfying PE=δ0​. Put E(x)=e−∣x∣/2. Away from zero, E′′=E; its first derivative has jump −1 at zero. Distributional differentiation therefore gives E′′=E−δ0​, and
(−D2+1)E=δ0​.​
(65)
For an ansatz u=etv, the forced equation becomes (1−D2)v=ϕ. With Fourier convention v(k)=∫e−ikxv(x)dx, its unique solution in the Schwartz space is
v(k)=1+k2ϕ​(k)​,v=E∗ϕ.​
(66)
The smooth multiplier and its derivatives have polynomial bounds, so this quotient is Schwartz. For uniqueness, multiplication of the difference's Fourier transform by 1+k2 gives zero, forcing the difference to vanish.
Subtract this particular solution and evolve the remaining initial data by the heat kernel:
u(t,x)=etv(x)+Ht​∗(f−v)(x).​
(67)
For smooth bounded f, the second term remains uniformly bounded, so e−tu(t,⋅)→v uniformly. If additionally f−v is integrable, its uniform norm is O(t−1/2), so the remainder itself decays. General bounded data need not have a decaying heat remainder, and no such stronger claim follows without a condition on the data. The homogeneous uniqueness assertion is understood in the bounded or usual tempered-growth solution class; the uniqueness of the particular Schwartz ansatz is unconditional within that stated class.

H=ℏω(a†a+21​).​

The number operator N=a†a is nonnegative because ⟨ψ,Nψ⟩=∥aψ∥2. The commutators [N,a]=−a and [N,a†]=a† lower and raise an eigenvalue by one. If an eigenvalue were a noninteger ν≥0, repeated lowering would produce a nonzero eigenvector with eigenvalue between zero and one, and one further lowering would have negative eigenvalue; its norm is nonzero because ∥aψ∥2=ν∥ψ∥2. This contradicts nonnegativity. Thus only nonnegative integers are allowed. The normalized Gaussian solves a∣0⟩=0, and raising it supplies every level, with
En​=ℏω(n+21​),∣n⟩=(a†)n∣0⟩/n!​.​

Thus the excited states never have a finite maximum capacity at a positive temperature: every finite prescribed density can be accommodated with a strictly negative chemical potential. The ground-state occupation then stays finite as area tends to infinity and its fraction vanishes. Hence there is no Bose-Einstein condensation at any positive temperature in this homogeneous ideal two-dimensional gas. At exactly zero temperature the ground state is occupied; the printed phrase about any temperature is understood as absence of a nonzero critical temperature, not exclusion of that zero-temperature limit.
